items.name: git-guardrails-claude-code
items.author: mattpocock
items.description: Prevent Claude Code from accidentally running destructive git commands like force push, hard reset, or clean.
items.summary: git-guardrails-claude-code sets up a Claude Code PreToolUse hook that intercepts and blocks dangerous git commands before the agent executes them. It copies a bundled block-dangerous-git.sh script into .claude/hooks/ (project) or ~/.claude/hooks/ (global), makes it executable, and registers it in settings.json under hooks.PreToolUse with a Bash matcher. Blocked commands include git push in all variants, reset --hard, clean -f/-fd, branch -D, and checkout ./restore .; when blocked, Claude sees a message that it lacks authority for those commands. The skill asks for scope, offers to customize the blocked-pattern list, and verifies the hook by piping a sample git push payload through the script. Developers reach for it when they want a hard technical stop on destructive git operations rather than trusting agent judgment.

High-impact rules include architecture-avoid-boolean-props, architecture-compound-components, state-decouple-implementation, state-context-interface, state-lift-state, patterns-explicit-variants, and patterns-children-over-render-props. The skill helps teams replace mode-switching props with explicit variant components, provider-owned state interfaces, and clearer extension points for future features.

items.name: writing-beats
items.author: mattpocock
items.description: Turn raw research notes, transcripts, or bullet points into a compelling narrative article one beat at a time.
items.summary: writing-beats is an exploit-phase writing skill that assembles a fixed markdown pile of raw material into an article as a journey of beats, choose-your-own-adventure style. It first settles prerequisites with the user (what the audience knows walking in), then offers 2-3 candidate starting beats drawn from the pile; after each pick it writes only that beat to the article file, re-reads the file from disk, and offers 2-3 reachable next beats, noting what each grounds. A grounding system enforces that no beat leans on a concept the audience has not met: every concept is either a prerequisite or introduced by an earlier beat, and picking a beat that grounds a concept unlocks the beats waiting on it. A beat is one move - a sentence, a paragraph, or a self-contained vignette - and the journey ends when complete, not when the pile is empty. Developers reach for it after an explore phase (such as writing-fragments) has produced the raw material and the article's path should be chosen interactively.

items.summary: writing-shape is an exploit-phase writing skill that turns a fixed markdown pile of raw material - fragments, unstructured prose, or a transcript - into an article, paragraph by paragraph, in a separate document; the raw file is read-only. Its 6-step loop reads the pile end-to-end, settles what the reader knows walking in, drafts 2-3 candidate openings that each imply a different thesis, then grows the article block by block, asking what the reader needs to hear next and arguing the form of each block (prose, list, table, callout, quote, code) deliberately. A grounding discipline blocks any paragraph from leaning on a concept the reader has not met, and the conversational stance is a grilling session inverted: weak transitions and paragraphs that do not earn their place get cut. Blocks are appended immediately and the file is re-read before every write to preserve user edits. Developers reach for it when raw notes or a transcript need to become one coherent, argued article.

items.summary: writing-fragments is the explore half of a two-phase writing workflow: it widens the space of what could be written without committing to structure, which is a separate exploit skill's job. It runs a grilling interview about whatever the user wants to write, and as fragments emerge from either side of the conversation it appends them to a single markdown file, separated by horizontal rules, starting from the very first prompt. Fragments are deliberately heterogeneous - sharp sentences, claims with one-line justifications, vignettes, half-thoughts, quotes, and especially a leading word, a compact coinage the whole piece can hang on, modeled on the novelist's diary of unstructured noticings. Developers reach for it at the start of an article, before writing-shape or writing-beats mine the pile.

items.name: migrate-to-shoehorn
items.author: mattpocock
items.description: Automatically update TypeScript test files that rely on unsafe `as` type assertions by replacing them with type-safe partial objects from @total-typescript/shoehorn.
items.summary: migrate-to-shoehorn converts TypeScript test files from `as` type assertions to the @total-typescript/shoehorn library, which lets tests pass partial data while keeping TypeScript happy. The workflow gathers requirements (which test files hurt, whether large objects or intentionally wrong data are involved), installs the package, greps *.test.ts and *.spec.ts for `as` assertions, then rewrites `as Type` to fromPartial() and `as unknown as Type` to fromAny(), adding imports and finishing with a type check. The doc maps each helper to a use case: fromPartial for partial data that still type-checks, fromAny for intentionally wrong data with autocomplete, fromExact to force a full object. It is strictly for test code, never production. Developers reach for it when faking large objects in tests means stubbing dozens of irrelevant properties.
highlights: Replaces `as Type` with fromPartial() and `as unknown as Type` with fromAny() across test files
Lets tests pass partial objects (e.g. only body.id of a 20-property Request) while still type-checking
Test code only - the doc explicitly forbids shoehorn in production code
Finds candidates with grep for ' as [A-Z]' in *.test.ts and *.spec.ts files
Three helpers: fromPartial (partial data), fromAny (intentionally wrong data), fromExact (force full object)

items.name: loop-me
items.author: mattpocock
items.description: Extends skill capabilities for developers.
items.summary: loop-me runs a stateful grilling session whose only output is workflow specs, stored one per file in workflows/*.md. It views the user's life as loops - recurring patterns in a career, a week, a morning, or a single repeated activity - and specifies each loop worth delegating as a workflow, proposing loops the user has not noticed. Specs draw on a shared vocabulary reached for only when a workflow calls for it: triggers (event or schedule), checkpoints (human-in-the-loop decision points), push right (defer the checkpoint as far as it will go), and briefs (tight decision-ready summaries, never raw output). It interviews the user relentlessly, one question at a time with a recommended answer attached, records the user's tools, channels, and terminology in NOTES.md, and keeps grilling until an implementer agent could build each spec without asking a single question.
highlights: Runs a stateful grilling session: relentless, one question at a time, with a recommended answer attached to each
Uses the loop lens: recurring patterns in the user's career, week, or morning reveal activities predictable enough to de
Shared 4-term vocabulary applied only when needed: trigger (event or schedule), checkpoint, push right, and brief
Definition of done: an implementer agent could build the spec without asking a single question
Maintains NOTES.md with the user's tools, channels, and canonical terminology, interviewing them about their world first
